analogy.p: A detective does not describe the room; they look for details that reveal what happened and who is responsible: a torn curtain, a stopped clock. A grade 9 reader looks for the small words, rhythm breaks and images that reveal the character’s mind and the writer’s purpose. The analogy breaks down because a detective seeks one fixed truth, whereas a literary reader can offer more than one valid interpretation.
analogy.t: Reading an extract like a detective at a crime scene

bullets: The extract is short and chosen because it is rich in language and important to the play.
The question names a focus, such as a character, an idea or a relationship; your whole answer must keep to it.
Part (a) is about the extract; part (b) will ask about the same theme elsewhere in the play, using recalled quotations.
Because the paper is closed book, the extract is the only text printed, so use it fully.
You are not being asked to summarise the extract or retell the scene.
Examiners reward coverage of the whole extract in a sensible order, with focus on the writer’s methods.

callouts.p: Whatever scene is printed, the steps are the same: place it, read it for shifts, annotate, argue, plan by the extract’s shape, then write with zoom and structure.
Mark totals and AO allocation for each part should be checked on your paper; do not rely on a remembered breakdown.

core.p: Part (a) of the Macbeth question gives you a printed extract and asks you to explore how Shakespeare presents a theme or character in it. The extract is your evidence, so the question is an exercise in close reading: AO2 (language, form, structure) matters most, supported by AO1 argument and, where it adds meaning, AO3 context. Check the marks and the AOs for this part on your own paper and specimen materials, as the weighting can differ between parts (a) and (b).

bullets: Place it: which act and scene? What happens just before and after? Who is on stage?
Read twice: first for what is happening; second for shifts in tone, rhythm, speaker or idea.
Annotate: underline powerful words and images, mark rhythm changes, note stage action and structure.
Thesis: write one sentence that says how Shakespeare presents the focus in this extract.
Plan: divide the extract into beginning, middle and end; choose one or two quotations for each part.
Write: use the zoom (claim, quote, word, structure, context, purpose) in each paragraph.
Check: spellings of names, accuracy of quotations, a final purpose sentence.

callouts.p: Open with your thesis straight away; do not paraphrase the question or the scene. A one or two sentence introduction is enough.

core.h: Step by step: from first read to final paragraph
core.p: A fixed routine saves time and gives you confidence under pressure. It has six stages: place, read twice, annotate, thesis, plan, write. Practise it on unfamiliar extracts until it is automatic. Each stage is short; the goal is to arrive at the writing stage with an argument and evidence already chosen.

callouts.p: Highlight single words (verbs, adjectives, nouns with strong connotations). Choose the three or four most productive for your plan.

core.p: Annotation is a hunt for evidence that supports your thesis. Do not annotate everything; look for patterns and shifts. Focus on words that carry unusual connotations, repeated images and changes in sentence length or rhythm. Note where the extract begins and ends and what it does to the audience at those points. Use three tags: language, structure and form, context.

head: Look for
Macbeth example
What to say
rows: Authority, desperation; character trying to control events
Motifs build theme across the play
Short phrases in 2.2; long breaths in 1.7
“A little water clears us of this deed”
Calm to panic; plan to doubt

bullets: Beginning: the first image, tone, speaker or action. What expectation does it set?
Middle: the development, build, shift or complication. What changes?
End: the final line, couplet, exit or image. What is the last effect on the audience?
Link paragraphs with structural words: “The extract opens…”, “The mood shifts…”, “By the end…”.
Quote from each part so that the whole extract is covered.
Where useful, mention what the extract shows about the play’s wider development, but keep this brief.

callouts.p: It shows you understand structure (AO2) and keeps you from jumping around or missing the ending.

core.p: An extract has a shape. Examiners reward answers that follow it, because that shows you understand how Shakespeare builds an effect. The simplest approach is to treat the beginning, middle and end as three paragraphs, each with a main idea and one or two quotations. For a long extract you might split the middle into two, but avoid more than four body paragraphs.

bullets: Iambic pentameter: ten syllables, five beats (ta-DUM). Steady rhythm suggests control; irregular lines suggest panic.
Broken or shared lines: two characters share one verse line, creating urgency and tension.
Enjambment: a sentence runs over the line end, giving a feeling of rush or overflow.
Caesura: a pause in a line, creating shock or hesitation.
Rhyming couplets: often close a scene, giving a sense of resolution or a decision.
Prose: the Porter, the Doctor and Gentlewoman, and Lady Macbeth sleepwalking; prose signals a break from formal verse.
Soliloquy and aside: show private thoughts; place them in the structure of the play.

callouts.p: Only mention rhythm if it is visible on the page of your extract. “The line is broken, suggesting hesitation” needs evidence of a short or shared line.

core.h: Writing about verse, prose and form
core.p: Form is part of meaning. Macbeth is mostly in blank verse, which is unrhymed iambic pentameter, the rhythm closest to natural speech. When the rhythm breaks, shortens or changes, the audience feels the character’s state of mind. The witches use rhyming trochaic tetrameter, which sounds like a chant. Prose is used for low-status characters and for moments of mental collapse. Learning to name and interpret these patterns gives you quick AO2 points.

bullets: Embed the quotation in your own sentence: “She asks the spirits to “unsex” her, a command that…”.
Keep quotations short: one to six words, often a single word.
Name the technique only when you can explain its effect.
Aim for three or four substantial paragraphs, not six thin ones.
Finish the answer with a purpose sentence rather than repeating your thesis.

callouts.p: ‘The verb unsex is a command; Lady Macbeth does not ask but orders the spirits, which shows determination, though the need for the command hints at doubt.’

core.h: Writing the paragraph: models and starters
core.p: Each paragraph needs a claim, a short quotation, an analysis of a word or technique, a structural note, and a link to context or audience. The paragraph should read as an argument, not a list of devices. A grade 9 paragraph often contains an alternative interpretation, which shows a sophisticated reading.

head: Move
Starter or model sentence
rows: The mood shifts when… as shown by…
A Jacobean audience, who believed…, would…
Ultimately, this makes the audience feel/think…

callouts.p: Examiners can tell. Use your knowledge of the scene to speed your annotation, but let the printed words drive your analysis.

core.h: Typical extracts and what to say
core.p: Certain scenes appear again and again because they are pivotal. Practising each one with the method gives you a stock of ideas and quotations, even when the printed extract is different. The table gives the focus and key language to look for. Always read the actual printed extract first; do not force a pre-learned answer onto it.

head: Extract
Likely focus
Language to look for
rows: Paradox, prophecy, Macbeth’s start and aside
Act 2 Sc 1 and Sc 2: dagger and murder
“Avaunt! and quit my sight!”; broken lines
Riddling prophecy; “Double, double toil and trouble”
Prose; “Out, damned spot”; “All the perfumes of Arabia”
Repetition; “brief candle”; “a tale told by an idiot”

bullets: Weakness: paraphrasing the extract. Fix: after each quotation, ask “So what? What does this word suggest?”.
Weakness: listing techniques. Fix: choose three techniques and explain each effect fully.
Weakness: ignoring the end of the extract. Fix: plan so that your last paragraph covers the final lines.
Weakness: forced context. Fix: only use context that changes the meaning of a word or moment.
Weakness: running out of time. Fix: practise timed paragraphs; plan with shorthand.
Weakness: over-long quotations. Fix: short, precise phrases embedded in your sentences.

callouts.p: After writing, circle every quotation and check you have zoomed in on at least one word in each; add a purpose sentence at the end of each paragraph.

core.h: Common weaknesses and how to fix them
core.p: Many answers fail not because they lack ideas but because they lack focus and precision. Use the list below as a revision checklist. It is especially useful to rewrite one of your own paragraphs in each style: first as a typical weak paragraph, then as a grade 9 version.

plan: Middle 1: commands to the spirits: unsexing and blocking remorse
Middle 2: inversion of the feminine: milk and gall; “murdering ministers”
End: darkness and the fear of being seen: “blanket of the dark”
Context woven in: gender, witchcraft and heaven’s watching eye
essays.q: Explore how Shakespeare presents Lady Macbeth’s determination in this extract. (Demonstration extract: Act 1 Scene 5, the soliloquy that begins “The raven himself is hoarse”.)
essays.text:
In this extract Shakespeare presents Lady Macbeth’s determination as an act of violent self-redefinition. She attempts to rewrite her own nature by commanding the supernatural, but the extreme language she needs betrays the conscience she is trying to silence.

The soliloquy opens with a decision disguised as an omen: “The raven himself is hoarse”. By treating the raven, a bird associated with death, as already croaking Duncan’s arrival, Lady Macbeth makes the murder sound fated, and she places nature on her side. Because this is a soliloquy, there is no one to deceive, so the audience hears her true intentions; the abruptness of the opening, without a pause, suggests that her mind has already moved from receiving the news to planning.

The central movement of the extract is a series of imperatives. Her call on the spirits to “unsex me here” is striking because the verb “unsex” sounds almost coined, and she is giving an order, not making a plea. The phrase suggests that she associates femininity with weakness and cruelty with masculine power, a view shaped by Jacobean expectations of gender in which women’s influence was limited. She follows with “make thick my blood”, a request for a physical change. The sibilant listing of how she will “stop up the access and passage to remorse” sounds like an engineer blocking a pipe, so that conscience is treated as a mechanical fault. Yet a reader may notice that she needs this blocking at all, which could suggest that she expects to feel remorse unless she is transformed.

Shakespeare then pushes her language towards inversion. She asks the spirits to take her milk for gall, replacing the nourishment associated with motherhood with bitterness, and she calls the spirits “murdering ministers”. The alliteration makes the phrase heavy and ritualistic, and “ministers” gives evil a religious function, a parody of a church. The apostrophe turns the soliloquy into an invocation; for a Jacobean audience, familiar with James I’s concerns about witchcraft, calling on spirits would have been a sinful act, placing her in the same moral world as the witches.

The extract closes by moving from the body to the sky. She calls on night to hide her “keen knife” and to prevent heaven from peeping “through the blanket of the dark” to cry “Hold, hold!” The domestic image of a blanket makes the violence feel eerily ordinary, and personifying heaven as a spying watcher shows her trying to blind God. Yet the line also suggests that she fears being stopped, as if the possibility of a voice crying “Hold, hold!” is real. The extract ends on this interrupted cry, leaving the audience with the sense that her determination is a performance of courage against an inner doubt.

Overall, Shakespeare presents Lady Macbeth as a figure whose will is real but whose conscience is not extinguished. Her determination is dramatised through commands, but the intensity of those commands suggests the effort needed to sustain them.
essays.thesis: In this extract Shakespeare presents Lady Macbeth’s determination as a violent act of self-redefinition: she tries to rewrite her own nature by commanding the supernatural, but the very need to blind herself and block remorse exposes the conscience she is trying to deny.
why: AO1: a clear conceptual thesis (self-redefinition versus exposed conscience) developed from beginning to end of the extract, with a considered alternative reading.
AO2: zooms in on single words (“unsex”, “ministers”, “blanket”), names techniques precisely (imperative, apostrophe, alliteration, personification) and comments on structure within the extract.
AO3: context woven into the analysis (Jacobean gender roles, belief in witchcraft, heaven’s watching eye) as explanation, not a list.
The answer follows the shape of the extract in order (beginning, middle, end) without narrating, and ends on Shakespeare’s purpose.
AO4: controlled, varied sentences and accurate spelling; short embedded quotations.

quotes.a: The raven, a bird of ill omen, is said to be hoarse with croaking about Duncan’s arrival. Lady Macbeth begins by reading nature as an ally of her plan. Starting a soliloquy with an omen introduces the supernatural tone before the invocation proper. The image also makes her seem already in tune with darkness, so her cruelty feels both natural to her and unnatural to us.
quotes.c: Ravens were associated with death and witchcraft.
quotes.ref: Act 1 Sc 5, opening of Lady Macbeth’s soliloquy

quotes.a: The imperative “unsex” commands spirits to remove her femininity, which she associates with weakness. The coined-sounding verb makes the request unnatural, and “here” suggests it should happen at once. This is a key example for extract questions because you can zoom on a single word, then widen to gender, power and the supernatural.
quotes.ref: Act 1 Sc 5, early in the soliloquy

quotes.a: She asks for her blood to be thickened so that pity cannot flow. Blood motif begins here, and “thick” suggests sluggish, unfeeling. The sibilance and plosives in “stop up the access and passage to remorse” follow, so the whole passage sounds like a physical blocking of conscience. Alternative reading: the request shows she expects to feel remorse unless she blocks it.
quotes.c: Bodily humours: thick blood meant cold cruelty.

quotes.a: She addresses the spirits as “ministers”, servants who carry out murder. The alliteration of “m” makes the phrase heavy and ritualistic, and “ministers” has a religious ring, so evil parodies the church. The apostrophe turns the soliloquy into an invocation, a spell-like speech that mirrors the witches.
quotes.c: Witchcraft belief; invoking spirits as a crime.
quotes.ref: Act 1 Sc 5, Lady Macbeth’s soliloquy, middle

quotes.a: Darkness is imagined as a blanket that can hide the crime from heaven. The domestic image of a bed blanket contrasts with the violence it covers, so the ordinary becomes sinister. Heaven “peeping” is personified as a curious watcher, so she tries to blind God. The image launches the play’s motif of darkness and concealment.
quotes.ref: Act 1 Sc 5, closing lines of the soliloquy

quotes.a: Macbeth feels that half the world is under the spell of sleep and nightmares, and Nature itself seems dead. The hush of the scene, with short phrases and hard consonants, builds suspense. It sets the scene for murder and pre-echoes the disorder of Act 2 Sc 4. A reader can see it as a reflection of his inner state projected on the world.
quotes.c: The Great Chain of Being: disorder in nature.

quotes.a: Macbeth imagines his bloody hand turning every ocean red. The polysyllabic Latinate diction (“multitudinous”, “incarnadine”) gives the line a grand, hyperbolic sweep, and then the monosyllabic “Making the green one red” follows. The contrast between ornate and plain shows a mind struggling to absorb the horror. Zooming in on “incarnadine” gives you a strong AO2 point.
quotes.c: Blood guilt as indelible; echoed in Act 5.
quotes.t: hyperbole, polysyllabic diction, contrast, blood imagery

quotes.a: Macbeth commands the ghost to go in archaic, imperative language. The exclamation marks and short phrases mimic a panicked outburst, which breaks the banquet’s formality. The command shows he is trying to reassert kingship over a spirit, but the audience sees his authority failing. A staging choice (whether the ghost appears) affects meaning.
quotes.c: Ghosts as spirits or guilty conscience.
quotes.ref: Act 3 Sc 4, Macbeth to Banquo’s ghost

quotes.a: Macbeth voices the belief that murder will lead to more murder, or to punishment. The repeated word “blood” in a short proverb-like sentence makes it sound like a law of the universe. It is a moment of recognition within a scene of disorder, and it shows he sees where his path leads but continues.
quotes.c: Revenge and divine justice in Jacobean thought.
quotes.ref: Act 3 Sc 4, Macbeth after the ghost leaves

quotes.a: She says that all the perfumes of Arabia will not sweeten her hand. The exotic image highlights how luxurious scents are powerless against guilt. Her speech is in prose, short, repetitive and disordered, which marks the collapse of control. The line completes the blood and cleansing motif begun in Act 2.
quotes.c: Guilt and damnation; the hand as sign of sin.

summary: Learn a step-by-step method for the part (a) extract question on Macbeth: place the extract in the play, annotate language, structure and context, build a thesis, plan three or four paragraphs that follow the extract’s shape, and write precise analysis that reaches grade 9.

terms.d: A short passage taken from the play and printed on the exam paper.
Unrhymed iambic pentameter, the usual rhythm of Shakespeare’s noble characters.
A command form of a verb, such as “come” or “unsex”.
A direct address to an absent person, spirit or thing.
When a sentence or phrase runs over the end of a line without a pause.
A pause within a line of verse, often marked by punctuation.
A verse line split between two speakers, creating a rapid exchange.
Two consecutive rhyming lines, often used to close a scene.
An instruction about action, entrances and exits or sound effects in the script.
